profile.feeling: Everyday; in figurative use, being consumed by something.

senses.def: to consume, eat up (figuratively: worry, jealousy)

examples.tr: What do you eat for breakfast?
She eats a lot of vegetables.

phrases.meaning: he was eaten up by regret or worry
I got into trouble, I paid for it

synonyms.nuance: to dine — elevated, literary
to gobble, eat greedily (mocking)

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔakal-. Compare Aramaic אֲכַל (ʾăḵal), Arabic أَكَلَ (ʔakala).

funFacts: אֹכֶל (okhel, food) and מַאֲכָל (ma’akhal, dish) come from the same root א־כ־ל.
pitfalls: The present tense agrees in gender: a man says אֲנִי אוֹכֵל, a woman אֲנִי אוֹכֶלֶת.
Future יֹאכַל: the א is silent (yokhal).
subtleties: Slang אָכַלְתִּי אוֹתָהּ has nothing to do with food: ‘I got burned’.

profile.feeling: Water in the heat, coffee in the morning; on its own, often alcohol.

examples.tr: What do you (f.) drink in the morning?

synonyms.nuance: to sip, take a gulp
to gulp down, drink in one go

etymology.text: Compare Aramaic אִשְׁתִּי (ʾištī), Ge’ez ሰትየ (sätyä).

funFacts: מִשְׁתֶּה (a feast, literally “a drinking”), the word for the banquets of the Purim story, comes from the same root.
pitfalls: A lamed-he verb: the present ends in a vowel — שׁוֹתֶה (m), שׁוֹתָה (f); the feminine has no -ֶת ending like אוֹכֶלֶת.
Infinitive לִשְׁתּוֹת (lishtot), with a dagesh in the ת.
subtleties: Without an object, הוּא שׁוֹתֶה can mean “he drinks (alcohol)” — as in English.

profile.feeling: The market, the supermarket, the shopping list.

senses.def: to acquire, to obtain (formal; wisdom, a friend)
to accept as true, to “buy” (a story)

examples.tr: I (m.) buy bread at the grocery shop.
She buys fruit at the market.

examples.text: אֲנִי לֹא קוֹנֶה אֶת הַסִּפּוּר הַזֶּה.

phrases.meaning: make the effort to find a true friend
he won him over, captivated him

synonyms.nuance: to acquire, purchase — written, commercial and official language

etymology.text: Cognate with Aramaic קְנָא (“to acquire”).

funFacts: The present participle is also a noun: קוֹנֶה “buyer, customer”.
Same letters, a different word: קָנֶה “reed, cane” — related to Greek κάννα and to English cane, canal, cannon.
pitfalls: A lamed-he verb like שָׁתָה: קוֹנֶה (m), קוֹנָה (f), קוֹנִים, קוֹנוֹת.
Do not confuse קוֹנָה “(she) buys” with קָנְתָה “she bought”.
subtleties: In the Bible and in formal Hebrew קָנָה means “acquire” in general, not only with money: קְנֵה לְךָ חָבֵר.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses אָהַב only as “to love”; in Modern Hebrew the same verb is the normal way to say “like” for food and activities (אֲנִי אוֹהֵב חֲצִילִים), and the profile shows both senses.

profile.feeling: From “I like salad” to “I love you” — one verb for both.

examples.tr: I love you (a man to a woman).

phrases.tr: and you shall love your neighbour as yourself

synonyms.nuance: to be fond of, to like (people or things) — milder than אָהַב
“dying on” — to be crazy about: אֲנִי מֵת עַל חֲצִילִים
“found favour in my eyes” = I like it; the thing liked is the subject: הַסָּלָט מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינַי

etymology.text: Compare Ugaritic 𐎀𐎅𐎁 (ảhb).

funFacts: Hebrew uses one verb for “like” and “love”: אֲנִי אוֹהֵב חֲצִילִים and אֲנִי אוֹהֵב אוֹתָךְ.
אַהֲבָה (love) and אָהוּב (beloved) come from the same root.
pitfalls: A definite object needs אֶת: אֲנִי אוֹהֵב אֶת הַסָּלָט — but אֲנִי אוֹהֵב סָלָט.
Plural with hataf patah: אוֹהֲבִים, אוֹהֲבוֹת.
subtleties: For people אוֹהֵב is strong (“love”); to say you simply like someone, Hebrew prefers מְחַבֵּב.

profile.feeling: Wishes, orders at the counter, children asking for ice cream.

senses.def: to accept, to be pleased with (Biblical)

examples.tr: What do you (f.) want to eat?

phrases.tr: if you will it, it is no legend
phrases.meaning: determination can make a dream real

synonyms.nuance: “it comes to me” = I feel like (it): בָּא לִי גְּלִידָה; the thing wanted is the subject
to desire, to wish — elevated style

etymology.text: Compare Arabic رَضِيَ (raḍiya).

funFacts: In the Bible רָצָה means “to be pleased with, to accept” — close to its Arabic relative رَضِيَ (raḍiya, “to be satisfied”); “to want” is the later meaning.
pitfalls: Homograph: רָצָה is also “(she) runs” (the present of רָץ). הוּא רָצָה (ratsá) = he wanted; הִיא רָצָה (rátsa) = she runs.
A lamed-he verb: רוֹצֶה (m), רוֹצָה (f).
subtleties: In shops Israelis often ask with אֶפְשָׁר …? (“is it possible …?”) — politer than אֲנִי רוֹצֶה.

lexemes.role: marks a definite direct object (no English equivalent): אֲנִי אוֹכֵל אֶת הַגֶּזֶר

profile.feeling: Pots on the stove on a Friday afternoon, before the Shabbat dinner.

senses.def: to cook (to make food with heat)
to boil, to stew (food in water — as opposed to frying or baking)

examples.tr: You boil the rice for twenty minutes.

collocations.tr: a cookbook (בִּשּׁוּל “cooking”, from the same root)

phrases.tr: you shall not cook a kid in its mother’s milk
phrases.meaning: the verse behind the Jewish rule never to cook or eat meat together with milk

synonyms.nuance: “to prepare” — any food, also cold dishes: הֵכִין סָלָט
“to make food” — the everyday way to say “cook” at home: מִי עוֹשֶׂה אֹכֶל?

etymology.text: Piʿel of the root ב־שׁ־ל (Wiktionary; verbal noun בִּשּׁוּל “cooking”). The same root gives the adjective בָּשֵׁל “ripe, mature”.

funFacts: Ripe fruit is “cooked” by the sun: בָּשֵׁל “ripe” has the same root ב־שׁ־ל.
Because of Exodus 23:19, kosher kitchens keep separate dishes for meat (בְּשָׂרִי) and for milk products (חָלָבִי).
pitfalls: The piʿel present starts with מְ־: מְבַשֵּׁל, מְבַשֶּׁלֶת, מְבַשְּׁלִים, מְבַשְּׁלוֹת — never *בּוֹשֵׁל.
The ב has a dot (b) at the start of בִּשֵּׁל (bishel) but not after מְ: מְבַשֵּׁל (mevashel, with v).
subtleties: English “cook” covers every way of making food; בִּשֵּׁל is first of all cooking with heat, in a pot. Baking is אָפָה, frying טִגֵּן.
A cook (the job) is a different word: טַבָּח.

profile.feeling: Fresh bread from the bakery — the basic food; in old texts, food and livelihood itself.

examples.tr: The children eat bread with cheese.
By the sweat of your brow you shall eat bread.

phrases.text: לֹא עַל הַלֶּחֶם לְבַדּוֹ יִחְיֶה הָאָדָם
phrases.tr: man does not live by bread alone

phrases.meaning: his daily routine, something he does or meets all the time

synonyms.nuance: “bread, a piece of bread” — old and formal (פַּת שַׁחֲרִית “morning bread”, the Rabbinic word for breakfast)

etymology.text: Cognate with Arabic لَحْم (laḥm, “meat”), with the varying semantic developments being due to the differing agriculture and diets of the Arabian Peninsula and the Fertile Crescent (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Bethlehem is בֵּית לֶחֶם, “house of bread”.
In Arabic the same word, لَحْم (laḥm), means “meat”: the staple of the farmers of the Fertile Crescent was bread, that of the herders of Arabia meat.
The blessing before a meal with bread ends with הַמּוֹצִיא לֶחֶם מִן הָאָרֶץ “who brings forth bread from the earth”.
pitfalls: As food it is uncountable: אֲנִי אוֹכֵל לֶחֶם (no “a”). One loaf is כִּכַּר לֶחֶם, or in a shop simply לֶחֶם אֶחָד; the plural לְחָמִים means loaves or kinds of bread.
Stress on the first syllable: LE-chem (like יֶלֶד, סֵפֶר).
subtleties: A bread roll is לַחְמָנִיָּה (from the same word); pitta is פִּתָּה; the plaited Shabbat bread is חַלָּה.

profile.feeling: Breakfast tables full of white cheeses — the soft גְּבִינָה לְבָנָה is an Israeli staple.

examples.tr: There are lots of cheeses here.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: kinds of cheese are named with גְּבִינָה + a word (גְּבִינָה צְהֻבָּה) or with loanwords (קוֹטֶג׳).

etymology.text: From the same root as Arabic جُبْن (jubn, “cheese”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: In a kosher kitchen cheese (חָלָבִי, dairy) is never eaten with meat (בְּשָׂרִי) — so a kosher restaurant serves no cheeseburgers.
In 2011 a consumer boycott over the price of קוֹטֶג׳ (cottage cheese) became a forerunner of Israel’s large social protests that summer.
pitfalls: Stress on the last syllable: g’vi-NA.
Feminine: גְּבִינָה טְעִימָה, הַגְּבִינָה הַזֹּאת.
subtleties: גְּבִינָה לְבָנָה is a soft spread, not a white hard cheese; hard cheese is גְּבִינָה צְהֻבָּה “yellow cheese”.

profile.feeling: The egg of the Israeli breakfast — fried, boiled or in a shakshuka.

examples.tr: He eats two eggs in the morning.
I (f.) buy eggs at the market.

collocations.tr: a fried egg, sunny side up (“eye egg”)

phrases.meaning: to tread very carefully (“walk on eggshells”)

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in everyday use (an omelette is a different word, חֲבִיתָה).

etymology.text: Uncertain, possibly named after its whiteness from the same root as أَبْيَض (ʔabyaḍ, “white”). Cognate with Arabic بَيْض (bayḍ) and Classical Syriac ܒܝܥܬܐ (bēʿṯā) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Shakshuka (שַׁקְשׁוּקָה), eggs poached in tomato sauce, came to Israel with the Jews of North Africa.
Arabic بَيْض (bayḍ) “eggs” is the same word.
pitfalls: Feminine, but the plural ends in -ִים: בֵּיצָה → בֵּיצִים — and it stays feminine: שְׁתֵּי בֵּיצִים, שָׁלוֹשׁ בֵּיצִים.
Same letters, another word: בִּצָּה “swamp” (unvowelled, both can be written ביצה).
In slang the plural בֵּיצִים also means “testicles” (vulgar) — context makes it clear.
subtleties: With a number it takes the feminine form: שָׁלוֹשׁ בֵּיצִים (not *שְׁלוֹשָׁה).

lexemes.note: Used as a mass noun; the plural בְּשָׂרִים (kinds of meat) is rare.

profile.feeling: Grilled meat at a holiday barbecue; in old texts “flesh” — the body and human frailty.

senses.def: flesh, body; humankind (בָּשָׂר וָדָם “flesh and blood”)

examples.tr: He is buying meat for the meal.
He is only flesh and blood.

collocations.tr: grilled meat, a barbecue (“meat on the fire”)

phrases.meaning: a mortal human being (as opposed to God)

phrases.tr: bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh
phrases.meaning: someone as close as one’s own body

profile.synonymsNone: No general synonym: kinds of meat are construct phrases (בְּשַׂר בָּקָר “beef”, בְּשַׂר כֶּבֶשׂ “lamb”).

etymology.text: From Proto-West Semitic *baśar-. Cognate to Arabic بَشَر (bašar, “human”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Arabic cognate بَشَر (bašar) means “human being” — Hebrew keeps that sense in בָּשָׂר וָדָם “a mortal”.
In kosher food בְּשָׂרִי “meaty” is a category: a בְּשָׂרִי meal has no milk products at all.
pitfalls: In a phrase the vowels change: בָּשָׂר → בְּשַׂר בָּקָר “beef”.
The letter is שׂ (sin, dot on the left): basar, not bashar.
subtleties: On menus בָּשָׂר usually means red meat; chicken (עוֹף) and fish (דָּגִים) are listed apart.

profile.feeling: Fish by the sea — grilled in a Jaffa restaurant, or gefilte fish on a holiday table.

examples.tr: Dad is cooking fish for dinner.
There are lots of fish here.

phrases.tr: the fish stinks from the head

synonyms.nuance: a Biblical collective noun, “the fish (of a river)”: וְהַדָּגָה אֲשֶׁר בַּיְאֹר מֵתָה (Exodus 7:21)

etymology.text: Related to Ugaritic 𐎄𐎂 (dg), of unknown ultimate origin (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Jonah was swallowed by a דָּג גָּדוֹל, “a big fish” — the Hebrew Bible never says “whale”.
The same letters are the verb דָּג “he fishes”; a fisherman is a דַּיָּג.
pitfalls: As a dish Hebrew often uses the plural: אֲנִי לֹא אוֹכֵל דָּגִים “I don’t eat fish”.
In a phrase the plural becomes דְּגֵי: דְּגֵי יָם “sea fish”.
subtleties: One fish on the plate is דָּג (אֲנִי אוֹכֵל דָּג); fish in general is דָּגִים.

profile.feeling: Chicken — the most common meat at Israeli tables: schnitzel, soup, the grill.

examples.tr: We are eating chicken and rice.
The chicken is in the oven.
The eagle is a big bird.

synonyms.nuance: “hen” — the live bird; for the meat Israelis say עוֹף
“bird” in everyday speech; עוֹף for “bird” is formal or zoological

etymology.text: Compare Ge’ez ዖፍ (ʿof, “bird”) (Wiktionary). The verb עָף “to fly” has the same root ע־ו־ף.

funFacts: Its basic meaning is “a flyer”: עָף “(he) flies” has the same root.
The phoenix is עוֹף הַחוֹל in Hebrew.
pitfalls: Masculine, with a plural in -וֹת: עוֹפוֹת.
With the article: הָעוֹף (hā-, before ע).
The live chicken is תַּרְנְגֹלֶת (hen) or תַּרְנְגוֹל (rooster); עוֹף is above all the meat.
subtleties: On a menu or in a recipe עוֹף is chicken meat in general: מְרַק עוֹף, שְׁנִיצֶל עוֹף.

lexemes.note: A mass noun with no everyday plural.

profile.feeling: Rice beside chicken and salad — an everyday side dish.

examples.tr: The children eat rice with chicken.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; it is a mass noun.

etymology.text: From Ancient Greek ὄρυζα (óruza), from an Eastern Iranian language (Wiktionary).

funFacts: A word you know: it comes from Greek ὄρυζα, like German Reis, English rice and Russian рис.
pitfalls: Everyday spelling with ו: אורז. Without it, ארז reads as אֶרֶז “cedar”.
With the article: הָאֹרֶז (hā- before א).
subtleties: Uncountable: אֲנִי אוֹכֵל אֹרֶז, קְצָת אֹרֶז — no plural in everyday use.

profile.feeling: A warm pot on a winter evening; chicken soup as comfort food.

examples.tr: In winter we eat a lot of soups.

synonyms.nuance: “broth, stock” — the clear liquid (צִיר עוֹף), not a whole soup

etymology.text: Cognate with Arabic مَرَق (maraq) and the more common Arabic مَرَقَة (maraqa) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic مَرَق (maraq) “broth” is the same word.
Hebrew “eats” soup, like Greek (τρώω σούπα), Russian (есть суп) and German (Suppe essen).
pitfalls: Soup is eaten, not drunk: אוֹכְלִים מָרָק (as German Suppe essen).
In a phrase the vowels shorten: מָרָק → מְרַק עוֹף; plural מְרָקִים.
subtleties: In Israeli winters soup is often the whole supper, and מְרַק עוֹף is the classic home remedy for a cold.

profile.feeling: Chopped cucumber and tomato — the “Israeli salad” at every meal, even at breakfast.

examples.tr: At the restaurant they first bring lots of salads.
I’m all mixed up (“I have a salad in my head”).

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: it is the general word for any salad (סָלָט יִשְׂרְאֵלִי, סָלַט חֲצִילִים).

etymology.text: Ultimately from Latin sal (Wiktionary) — “salted” greens.

funFacts: One word in all your languages: from Latin sal “salt”, like German Salat, Greek σαλάτα, Russian салат, Turkish salata and Arabic سَلَطَة (salaṭa).
pitfalls: Masculine: סָלָט טָעִים, הַסָּלָט הַזֶּה (not *טְעִימָה).
Before another noun the vowel shortens: סָלָט → סָלַט פֵּרוֹת “fruit salad”.
subtleties: The plural סָלָטִים is the array of small salads and dips served first in Israeli restaurants.

profile.feeling: Watermelon, figs and oranges — the sweet end of a meal in a sunny country.

examples.tr: She buys fruit at the market.

examples.text: הַסֵּפֶר הוּא פְּרִי שֶׁל עֲבוֹדָה קָשָׁה.
examples.tr: The book is the fruit of hard work.

phrases.tr: who creates the fruit of the tree
phrases.meaning: the end of the blessing said before eating fruit
wine, in the blessing over wine

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym (תְּנוּבָה “produce, yield” is formal and collective).

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *piry-. Cognate with Ge’ez ፍሬ (fəre) and Ugaritic 𐎔𐎗 (pr /pirû/) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Bible’s first commandment, פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ “be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:28), comes from the same root פ־ר־ה.
Tu BiShvat, the “New Year of the Trees”, is celebrated by eating fruit, especially dried fruit (פֵּרוֹת יְבֵשִׁים).
pitfalls: The plural changes its vowels and ends in -וֹת although the word is masculine: פְּרִי → פֵּרוֹת.
English uses “fruit” as a mass noun; Hebrew uses the plural: אֲנִי אוֹכֵל פֵּרוֹת “I eat fruit”.
Everyday spelling of the plural: פירות.
subtleties: One piece of fruit is פְּרִי אֶחָד; in botany a tomato is also a פְּרִי.

profile.feeling: Crisp apples — and apple dipped in honey for a sweet New Year.

examples.tr: The girl is eating an apple.
At Rosh Hashanah people eat apple dipped in honey.

phrases.tr: the apple does not fall far from the tree

synonyms.nuance: “tree apple” — the full name, which keeps it apart from תַּפּוּחַ אֲדָמָה “potato”

etymology.text: Uncertain; if derived from a verbal root then either named after its scent (נָפַח “to blow, to scent”) or from תָּפַח “to swell, become round”. Cognates include Arabic تُفَّاح (tuffāḥ) and Ugaritic tpḥ (Wiktionary).

funFacts: תַּפּוּחַ אֲדָמָה “earth apple” is a potato — like French pomme de terre and Austrian German Erdapfel.
תַּפּוּז “orange” is a modern blend of תַּפּוּחַ זָהָב “golden apple”.
Arabic تُفَّاح (tuffāḥ) is the same word.
pitfalls: The final ח is said after an extra a: ta-pu-ach (a “stolen patah”).
Do not mix it up with תַּפּוּחַ אֲדָמָה “potato” (in speech often shortened to תַּפּוּד).
subtleties: Masculine: תַּפּוּחַ אֶחָד, שְׁנֵי תַּפּוּחִים, שְׁלוֹשָׁה תַּפּוּחִים.

lexemes.note: A mass noun with no everyday plural.

profile.feeling: A spoonful in the tea — and, colloquially, diabetes.
profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; the medical word for diabetes, סֻכֶּרֶת, is built from it.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar), borrowed from Middle Persian šakar, from Gandhari śakara, from Sanskrit शर्करा (śárkarā), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorkeh₂ (“gravel”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: One word through all your languages: Sanskrit śárkarā → Persian šakar → Arabic sukkar → Hebrew סֻכָּר; the same journey gave German Zucker, English sugar, Greek ζάχαρη, Russian сахар and Turkish şeker.
Diabetes is סֻכֶּרֶת, with the ending of names of illnesses, as in צַהֶבֶת “jaundice”.
pitfalls: Everyday spelling with ו: סוכר. Without it, סכר reads as סֶכֶר “dam”.
The ֻ (kubbutz) is an u: su-KAR.
subtleties: Uncountable: קְצָת סֻכָּר, הַרְבֵּה סֻכָּר; sugar cubes are קֻבִּיּוֹת סֻכָּר.

lexemes.note: A mass noun; the plural מְלָחִים is the chemists’ “salts”.

profile.feeling: Salt on the table — and the salty Dead Sea, יָם הַמֶּלַח.

senses.def: permanence, continuity (בְּרִית מֶלַח “a covenant of salt”)

examples.tr: He eats a lot of salt.

examples.text: יָם הַמֶּלַח הוּא הַמָּקוֹם הַנָּמוּךְ בְּיוֹתֵר בָּעוֹלָם.
examples.tr: The Dead Sea is the lowest place in the world.

etymology.text: From Proto-West Semitic *milḥ-. Compare Aramaic מִלְחָא (milḥā), Arabic مِلْح (milḥ), Maltese melħ (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Dead Sea is יָם הַמֶּלַח, “the Salt Sea”.
Arabic مِلْح (milḥ) is the same word; מַלָּח “sailor” only looks related — it comes from Akkadian.
pitfalls: Stress on the first syllable: ME-lach.
The plural מְלָחִים exists only in chemistry (“salts”); in the kitchen it is uncountable.
subtleties: Salt preserves, so בְּרִית מֶלַח, a “covenant of salt” (Numbers 18:19), is one that lasts for ever.

lexemes.note: Used only in the plural (masculine): הַמַּיִם קָרִים.

profile.feeling: Water in a hot climate: a bottle is always in the bag.

examples.tr: I (m.) drink a lot of water.
Could I have a glass of water, please?

phrases.text: מַיִם רַבִּים לֹא יוּכְלוּ לְכַבּוֹת אֶת הָאַהֲבָה

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *māy-. Compare Aramaic מַיָּא (mayyā), Arabic مَاء (māʔ). Doublet of מ״ם (the letter mem) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: It looks like a dual (-ַיִם, like שָׁמַיִם “sky”), but it is simply a noun used only in the plural.
The letter מ (mem) has the same name as water: its oldest shape was a wavy line of water.
Arabic مَاء (māʔ) is the same word.
pitfalls: Always plural: הַמַּיִם קָרִים “the water is cold” — never a singular.
Before another noun it becomes מֵי: מֵי בֶּרֶז “tap water”.
subtleties: In a café “a water” is כּוֹס מַיִם or בַּקְבּוּק מַיִם; “some water” is just מַיִם or קְצָת מַיִם.

profile.feeling: A glass of tea with fresh mint (נַעְנַע) in the afternoon.

examples.tr: Dad drinks tea in the morning.
Do you (f.) want tea or coffee?

synonyms.nuance: “an infusion” — herbal tea, the word on packets and menus

etymology.text: Borrowed from Western European languages, compare French thé and German Tee (Wiktionary).

funFacts: One Chinese word (茶) travelled two ways: by sea as “te” (Hebrew תֵּה, German Tee, English tea), overland as “cha” (Russian чай, Turkish çay, Greek τσάι, Arabic شَاي).
pitfalls: One short syllable: te (not “tea”).
Masculine: תֵּה חַם.
subtleties: Israelis often drink tea from a glass: כּוֹס תֵּה.

profile.feeling: Israeli café culture: a הָפוּךְ in the morning, black “mud” coffee with cardamom.

examples.tr: The coffee here is very good.

phrases.meaning: ground coffee brewed straight in the cup, Turkish style

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; kinds of coffee are named with loans (אֶסְפְּרֶסּוֹ) or Hebrew phrases (קָפֶה הָפוּךְ).

etymology.text: Borrowed from French café, from Italian caffè, from Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve), from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa, “coffee”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: From Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa) via Turkish kahve, Italian caffè and French café — the same chain gave German Kaffee, Greek καφές and Russian кофе.
קָפֶה הָפוּךְ, “upside-down coffee”, is the Israeli name for a latte.
pitfalls: Masculine: קָפֶה חַם, הַקָּפֶה הַזֶּה.
No plural in everyday use: “two coffees” is שְׁתֵּי כּוֹסוֹת קָפֶה.
subtleties: בֵּית קָפֶה “house of coffee” is a café.

profile.feeling: Milk in coffee and cereal; in the Bible, the promised land “flowing with milk and honey”.

examples.tr: Do you (f.) want coffee with milk?

phrases.tr: a land flowing with milk and honey

etymology.text: Cognate with Aramaic חַלְבָּא and sharing its root with Arabic حَلِيب (ḥalīb) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: From the same word comes חָלָבִי “dairy” — in kosher food a category kept apart from meat.
Arabic حَلِيب (ḥalīb) “milk” shares the root.
pitfalls: With the article: הֶחָלָב (he-, not ha-).
Same letters, another word: חֵלֶב “animal fat” (forbidden in the Torah).
subtleties: Before another noun the vowels shorten: חֲלֵב סוֹיָה, חֲלֵב שְׁקֵדִים.

profile.feeling: Fresh orange juice squeezed at a market stall.

examples.tr: I (m.) would like orange juice, please.

phrases.tr: took the juice out of him

synonyms.nuance: “must, new wine” — Biblical; today also the sweet grape juice used for kiddush

etymology.text: From Biblical Hebrew מִיץ (miṣ, “squeezing, pressing”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: In the Bible מִיץ meant “pressing, squeezing”; Modern Hebrew made it the word for juice.
pitfalls: Masculine: מִיץ קַר; plural מִיצִים.
The fruit after it is plural: מִיץ תַּפּוּזִים (“juice of oranges”).
subtleties: מִיץ טִבְעִי “natural juice” is the freshly squeezed kind; plain מִיץ may come from a carton.

profile.feeling: Wine for Kiddush on Friday night and four cups at the Passover Seder.

examples.tr: We are buying a bottle of wine.

examples.text: בְּלֵיל הַסֵּדֶר שׁוֹתִים אַרְבַּע כּוֹסוֹת יַיִן.
examples.tr: On Seder night people drink four cups of wine.

phrases.tr: wine goes in, a secret comes out

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in everyday use (Biblical poetry also has תִּירוֹשׁ “new wine”).

etymology.text: From Proto-West Semitic *wayn- (Wiktionary).

funFacts: *wayn- belongs to an old Mediterranean wine word, usually connected with Greek οἶνος and Latin vinum (→ German Wein, English wine).
The blessing over wine ends with בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הַגָּפֶן “who creates the fruit of the vine”.
pitfalls: The plural ends in -וֹת and changes the vowels: יַיִן → יֵינוֹת (kinds of wine).
Stress on the first syllable: YA-yin.
subtleties: As a drink it is uncountable: כּוֹס יַיִן; יֵינוֹת are kinds of wine (יֵינוֹת מֵהַגָּלִיל).

profile.feeling: A cold beer on the beach in Tel Aviv.

senses.def: a glass, bottle or can of beer

examples.tr: We would like two beers, please.

etymology.text: Borrowed from German Bier. The final ־ָה (-a) could have been added under the influence of Arabic بِيرَة (bīra) or Ottoman Turkish بیرا (bira) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: A word you know: it is German Bier, with an -a perhaps from Arabic or Turkish bira.
pitfalls: Homograph: בִּירָה is also “capital city” (bi-RA, as in בִּירַת צָרְפַת “the capital of France”); beer is BI-ra.
Feminine: בִּירָה קָרָה, שְׁתֵּי בִּירוֹת.
subtleties: Ordering, “a beer” is simply בִּירָה; “two beers” is שְׁתֵּי בִּירוֹת.

lexemes.note: A two-word lexeme (construct phrase), tokenized as one word; the article goes on its second word.

profile.feeling: The famous Israeli breakfast: eggs, salad, white cheese, olives and bread.

examples.tr: The hotel has an Israeli breakfast.

synonyms.nuance: “morning bread” — the old Rabbinic name for breakfast

etymology.text: Built from אֲרוּחָה “meal” (Wiktionary) in its construct form אֲרוּחַת “meal of”. + בֹּקֶר “morning” — “the meal of the morning”.

funFacts: The “Israeli breakfast” of the kibbutz dining halls — eggs, chopped salad, white cheese, olives, bread — became a hotel classic.
pitfalls: The article goes on the second word: אֲרוּחַת הַבֹּקֶר “the breakfast” (in speech you also hear the non-standard הָאֲרוּחַת בֹּקֶר).
Feminine, because of אֲרוּחָה: אֲרוּחַת בֹּקֶר טוֹבָה.
subtleties: “To have breakfast” is לֶאֱכֹל אֲרוּחַת בֹּקֶר — Hebrew has no verb like German frühstücken.

lexemes.note: A two-word lexeme (construct phrase), tokenized as one word; the article goes on its second word.

profile.feeling: The main hot meal of the day in Israel — at work, at school, at grandma’s.

synonyms.nuance: “noon” — alone it also means lunch: מָה יֵשׁ לַצָּהֳרַיִם? “what’s for lunch?”

etymology.text: Built from אֲרוּחָה “meal” (Wiktionary) in its construct form אֲרוּחַת “meal of”. + צָהֳרַיִם “noon”, cognate with Arabic ظُهْر (ẓuhr) and, in form, the dual of צֹהַר “opening for light”.

funFacts: צָהֳרַיִם “noon” has the dual ending -ַיִם; Arabic ظُهْر (ẓuhr), also the name of the noon prayer, is the same word.
pitfalls: Pronounced tso-ho-RA-yim: the first vowel is o (a “short qamats”).
The article goes on the second word: אֲרוּחַת הַצָּהֳרַיִם.
subtleties: In Israel lunch is traditionally the main hot meal; supper is often lighter, much like breakfast.

lexemes.note: A two-word lexeme (construct phrase), tokenized as one word; the article goes on its second word.

profile.feeling: Friday-night dinner with the family — the big meal of the week.

examples.text: בְּיוֹם שִׁשִּׁי יֵשׁ אֲרוּחַת עֶרֶב מִשְׁפַּחְתִּית.
examples.tr: On Friday there is a family dinner.

synonyms.nuance: a festive or ritual meal at any hour (סְעוּדַת שַׁבָּת, סְעוּדַת חַג)

etymology.text: Built from אֲרוּחָה “meal” (Wiktionary) in its construct form אֲרוּחַת “meal of”. + עֶרֶב “evening” (Wiktionary: עֶרֶב is cognate with Arabic غَرْب “west”).

funFacts: עֶרֶב “evening” and Arabic غَرْب (ḡarb) “west” are cognates: evening is when the sun goes west — the root behind “Maghreb”.
pitfalls: The article goes on the second word: אֲרוּחַת הָעֶרֶב (hā- before ע).
עֶרֶב is “evening”, the same word as in עֶרֶב טוֹב.
subtleties: The Friday-night meal opens with the blessing over wine (קִדּוּשׁ) and bread — the biggest family dinner of the week.
